newsitem.title: UK: Britain suspects IRA of army HQ blast - Mayhew.
newsitem.headline: Britain suspects IRA of army HQ blast - Mayhew.

text.p: Britain on Tuesday pointed the finger of suspicion at the Irish Republican Army (IRA) for an audacious car bomb attack inside its Northern Ireland army headquarters which injured 31 and shattered moves towards peace.
Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Patrick Mayhew said after a briefing from army and police security chiefs that the attack bore the hallmarks of the outlawed IRA.

Mayhew told a news conference the bombing at the base in Lisburn, near Belfast, in which two car bombs exploded, was "consistent with a terrorist organisation which declared a ceasefire in August, 1994".

The IRA, founded seven decades ago to rid the island of Ireland of its British colonial masters, called a truce in August two years ago in a vain attempt to get its political wing, Sinn Fein, invited to fledgling all-party peace talks.

Mayhew's comment was the most explicit allegation by a British government figure that the IRA carried out the attack, which raised fears that Protestant Loyalist gunmen, who want to keep Northern Ireland British, would end a truce of their own and kill Catholics in revenge.

The bombing was the first strike against security targets in Northern Ireland since the IRA and Loyalists called twin ceasefires in 1994 in response to Anglo-Irish attempts to convene talks on a lasting political settlement.

The bombs were planted inside the perimetre of the British army nerve centre, prompting an immediate review of security at what was supposed to be an impenetrable fortress for Britain's 18,000-strong force in Northern Ireland.
Twelve of the 31 injured were still in hospital on Tuesday, three in serious condition, police said. The blasts injured 20 soldiers and 11 civilians.
Martin McGuinness, top negotiator for Sinn Fein, brushed aside questions about whether the IRA was responsible and said the attack showed that a two-year-old Anglo-Irish peace initiative had failed.
"What we have to do is recognise how dangerous a situation we're in at the moment. There is a vacuum. It needs to be filled by real and meaningful peace negotiations," he said.

Sinn Fein is barred from the four-month-old peace talks in Belfast as punishment for the decision by the IRA to end its 17-month truce to dramatise its rejection of British demands that it start surrendering weapons to show good faith.
The British and Irish governments said they would press ahead with the peace talks and appealed to Loyalists, who have killed 900 Catholics to avenge IRA attacks, to keep their truce.

"There's no doubt whoever planted these devices were intent to try to blow the process that is taking place at the moment out of the water, and any challenge to a democratic process of that kind must be resisted," Britain's junior Northern Ireland Minister Michael Ancram told the BBC.
"I call on particularly the Loyalist paramilitaries not to fall into the trap of those who planted those devices with murderous intent and maintain their ceasefire," he said.

No group has claimed credit for the attack. The Irish Times newspaper quoted security sources as saying only the IRA had the expertise to breach the security cordon and detonate up to 1,000 lb (450 kg) of home-made fertiliser-based explosive.

There was speculation that a little-known breakaway Irish Republican group called the Continuity Army Council might claim responsibility for the attack, which would ease pressure on Sinn Fein and the Loyalist ceasefire.
The group abandoned a huge car bomb in Belfast last week. It is thought to be linked to a Dublin-based Republican group which broke from the mainstream movement about 20 years ago.
